# Kubernetes Pod PVC `$HOME` + tailnet/OTEL egress patterns

Research informing how to wire a tenant sandbox Pod in a 3-node k3s
homelab cluster (Longhorn 1.11 storage, Tailscale Operator, OTEL
Collector at `otel-collector.otel.svc.cluster.local:4317`) so that
(1) `$HOME` survives Pod restart via a PVC and (2) the Pod reaches the
in-cluster OTEL Collector through a default-deny NetworkPolicy that
already blocks RFC1918.

## Overview

For a tenant sandbox Pod that needs durable `$HOME` and OTLP/gRPC
telemetry to an in-cluster Collector, the cleanest configuration is:
**one StatefulSet (or Deployment) per operator with its own PVC**, on
**PodSecurity `restricted`** using `fsGroup` +
`fsGroupChangePolicy: OnRootMismatch` for non-root volume ownership, with
the Pod calling the **in-cluster Collector Service directly** (NOT the
tailnet hostname), gated by a NetworkPolicy that uses **namespaceSelector
+ podSelector** rather than `ipBlock` on the Collector ClusterIP.

The tailnet hostname remains the right answer for **external** callers
(existing usage by Claude wrappers) but is the wrong answer for in-cluster
Pod-to-Pod telemetry: documented MTU and performance collapse on the
exact k3s+Flannel+Tailscale topology [19], not-fixed graceful-failover
behavior for long-lived TCP streams [20], beta-status of the cluster-
egress feature [16], and architectural multi-hop overhead [16][17][18]
all push against the tailnet route. Detailed dimension analyses below.
Sources in [`citations.md`](citations.md).

## 1. PVC for `$HOME` — StatefulSet vs Deployment+PVC

See [references/pvc-statefulset-vs-deployment.md](references/pvc-statefulset-vs-deployment.md)
for full detail.

### StatefulSet semantics

A StatefulSet with `volumeClaimTemplates` creates one PVC per Pod, named
`{vct-name}-{sts-name}-{ordinal}` [1]. The PVC persists on Pod
restart/reschedule and re-binds to the new Pod ordinal automatically
[1]. By default, deleting or scaling a StatefulSet down does NOT delete
the PVCs:

> "Deleting and/or scaling a StatefulSet down will _not_ delete the
> volumes associated with the StatefulSet. This is done to ensure data
> safety, which is generally more valuable than an automatic purge of
> all related StatefulSet resources." [1]

`persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy` (alpha 1.23, beta 1.27) opts in
to automatic deletion via `whenDeleted: Delete` and/or `whenScaled:
Delete` [2]. Critically, `whenScaled: Delete` does NOT fire on Pod
restart — only on actual replica reduction:

> "PVCs are deleted immediately when their replica is no longer needed.
> Note this does not include when a Pod is deleted and a new version
> rescheduled... The PVC is deleted only when the replica is no longer
> needed as signified by a scale-down or StatefulSet deletion." [2]

A known bug (k/k #126919) breaks `whenScaled: Delete` when the
`OwnerReferencesPermissionEnforcement` admission plugin is enabled [12].
Fixed via PR #126920; verify your k3s version includes the fix before
relying on opt-in deletion.

### Deployment+PVC semantics

A Deployment with an explicit PVC reference works for N=1 but breaks at
N>1 for `ReadWriteOnce` volumes — the second replica cannot attach the
volume on a different node. Naming is author-chosen, not ordinal-derived.

### Multi-instance pattern: one controller per operator

For "N copies of the same workload, one per operator-user":

- **One StatefulSet with N replicas** couples PVC names to ordinals.
  Adding/removing operators is awkward; scale-down removes the highest
  ordinal, not necessarily the operator being deprovisioned.
- **One StatefulSet per operator** gives operator-named PVCs and clean
  controller-level create/delete.

**Recommended:** one controller per operator. The decision between
per-operator StatefulSet and per-operator Deployment is mostly cosmetic
at N=1; the StatefulSet's `volumeClaimTemplates` is preferred because it
auto-provisions and binds the PVC by name without separate manifest
plumbing [1][2].

### Reclaim policy interaction (important)

With Longhorn's default StorageClass at `Delete` reclaim, deleting the
PVC removes the PV and the underlying Longhorn volume [3]:

> "For volume plugins that support the `Delete` reclaim policy, deletion
> removes both the PersistentVolume object from Kubernetes, as well as
> the associated storage asset in the external infrastructure." [3]

Therefore: leave `persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy` at the default
`Retain`/`Retain` so accidental controller deletion does not cascade to
data loss. `kubectl delete pvc` warning is explicit:

> "Use caution when deleting a PVC, as it may lead to data loss." [4]

Backup strategy (Longhorn snapshots/backups) is orthogonal to controller
choice and out of scope for this research.

## 2. PVC permissions for non-root + PodSecurity profile

See [references/pvc-permissions-non-root.md](references/pvc-permissions-non-root.md)
for full detail.

### PSS baseline vs restricted (exact deltas)

Restricted adds five hard requirements beyond baseline [5]:

| Control | Baseline | Restricted |
|---|---|---|
| `allowPrivilegeEscalation` | not required | must be `false` |
| `runAsNonRoot` | not required | must be `true` |
| `capabilities.drop` | not required | must include `ALL` |
| `capabilities.add` | many allowed | only `NET_BIND_SERVICE` |
| `seccompProfile.type` | not required | `RuntimeDefault` or `Localhost` |

Volume types are restricted to an 8-entry allow-list under restricted:
`configMap`, `csi`, `downwardAPI`, `emptyDir`, `ephemeral`,
`persistentVolumeClaim`, `projected`, `secret` [5]. PVCs are allowed —
the profile constrains how the Pod runs, not whether it can use a PVC.

### fsGroup mechanics

`fsGroup` on the Pod's `securityContext` tells kubelet to chown the
mount to that GID and add it to the process's supplementary group
set [6]. Behavior is gated by the CSI driver's `fsGroupPolicy` [9]:

- `None`: silently no-op [9].
- `File`: kubelet applies fsGroup regardless of fsType/access mode [9].
- `ReadWriteOnceWithFSType`: applies only when `fsType` is set AND
  `accessModes` contains `ReadWriteOnce` [9].

Longhorn 1.11 CSI uses `ReadWriteOnceWithFSType` [10]. For Filesystem
mode + RWO + Pod `fsGroup: N`, kubelet `chown`s the mount to GID N
on first mount.

For **Block mode**, kubelet does NOT chown:

> "Kubelet never attempts to change the permission and ownership of the
> block device when making it available inside the container...
> Longhorn puts the block device into group id 6, which is typically
> associated with the 'disk' group." [10]

Pods using block-mode PVCs "must either set the group id 6 in the
`pod.spec.securityContext`, or run as root." [10]

### fsGroupChangePolicy

Introduced in k8s 1.20 [7]. `OnRootMismatch` skips the recursive `chown`
if the volume root's group/permissions already match the requested
fsGroup [6][7]:

> "Set `fsGroupChangePolicy` to 'OnRootMismatch' so if the root of the
> volume already has the correct permissions, the recursive permission
> change can be skipped." [7]

Without this, recursive chown "can be pretty expensive for larger
volumes with lots of small files, which causes pod startup to take a
long time." [7] Longhorn's KB explicitly recommends pairing fsGroup
with `OnRootMismatch` [11].

### Severe failure mode (k/k #118058)

A large CSI volume took **40 hours** to complete fsGroup chown [13]. A
second Pod attempting to redeploy with `OnRootMismatch` "remained
blocked waiting for the first pod's mount to complete, as volume
operations are serialized per volume" — the only documented workaround
was "restart kubelet so that the go routines would be cleared" [13].
For a fresh per-tenant sandbox PVC this is unlikely; for shared
filesystems with massive file counts the risk is real.

### initContainer `chown -R` under restricted

Incompatible. Every container in a restricted Pod, including init
containers, must satisfy `runAsNonRoot: true` [5][15]. A non-root init
container cannot `chown` files it doesn't own because restricted's
`capabilities.drop: [ALL]` removes `CAP_CHOWN` [5]. The traditional
"chown init" pattern requires baseline or a PSA exemption.

The clean workaround under restricted: **let kubelet do the chown via
fsGroup** — no init container needed.

### Recommendation

For tenant sandbox Pods on Longhorn 1.11 Filesystem-mode RWO PVCs:

- **Stay on `restricted`**, not baseline. Sandbox = untrusted code;
  baseline allows `seccomp: Unconfined` and skips
  `runAsNonRoot` [5]. Below threshold for sandbox.
- Pod `securityContext`:
  - `runAsNonRoot: true`
  - `runAsUser: <per-tenant-uid>`
  - `fsGroup: <per-tenant-gid>`
  - `fsGroupChangePolicy: OnRootMismatch`
- No init container required [6][7][10][11].
- The sandbox image must accept arbitrary runtime UID/GID (not hardcode
  file ownership at build time).

Block mode requires a different path (`supplementalGroups: [6]`); for
sandboxes running shell-like workloads Filesystem mode is correct [10][14].

## 3. Tailscale Operator — Pod-to-tailnet egress

See [references/tailscale-operator-egress.md](references/tailscale-operator-egress.md)
for full detail.

### How egress actually works

A cluster Pod does NOT dial a `*.<tailnet>.ts.net` address directly. The
Operator's egress model [16][17][18]:

1. User creates an `ExternalName` Service with
   `tailscale.com/tailnet-fqdn: <host>.<tailnet>.ts.net` annotation [16].
2. Operator creates a **single-replica StatefulSet** proxy Pod in the
   `tailscale` namespace, running `tailscaled` [18].
3. Operator creates a headless Service pointing at the proxy Pod and
   **mutates `spec.externalName`** on the user's Service to that
   headless Service's cluster-DNS name [18].
4. Inside the proxy Pod's network namespace (only), the Operator
   installs `iptables`/`nftables` DNAT rules that map the proxy's
   tailnet IP to forwarded traffic [17][18].

### What IP the tenant Pod sees at netfilter

The destination at the tenant Pod's egress chain is the **in-cluster
proxy Pod IP**, NOT a CGNAT 100.64.x address [16][17][18]. A
NetworkPolicy permitting CGNAT (`100.64.0.0/10` in `ipBlock`) does NOT
match this path — that range only appears on the proxy Pod's `tailscale0`
interface, beyond the tenant Pod's enforcement point.

### Feature status

Mixed signals: the operator overview page is silent on beta/GA [17],
but the cluster-egress how-to page explicitly says:

> "Exposing tailnet services to your Kubernetes cluster is currently in
> beta." [16]

Trust the per-feature page. Egress is beta.

### Known failure modes for OTLP/gRPC

**Performance collapse on the exact project topology.** k3s with
Flannel-over-Tailscale CNI plus the Tailscale Operator measured 2-3
Mbit/s versus 700-800 Mbit/s direct [19]. Root cause: MTU. Tailscale
pins MTU to 1280; cluster container interfaces default to 1500;
WireGuard encapsulation needs more than 1280 to carry a 1280 payload.
Documented workaround: lower MTU to 1200 on one end [19].

**Long-lived streams hang on proxy restart.** When a ProxyGroup replica
restarts:

> "the database connection will continuously resend data until it times
> out." [20]

**Status: closed as not planned** — Tailscale has elected not to fix
this graceful-failover gap [20]. OTLP gRPC is exactly this kind of
long-lived bidirectional stream.

**gRPC client-side resolver delay.** gRPC's default `dns:///` URI
scheme triggers DNS lookups that "time out" through Tailscale's
resolver, adding ~30s on first connect; fix is `passthrough:///` [21].
Mechanism applies to OTLP exporters generically.

**Operator regression #18631.** Tailscale 1.94.1 made a single
misconfigured egress Service crash the operator's egress proxy, taking
down ALL egress for the cluster [30]. Blast radius increased vs 1.92.5.

### Verdict

Tailnet egress is the right answer for callers **outside** the cluster
(external Claude wrappers, existing usage). For in-cluster Pod →
in-cluster OTEL Collector, the architectural multi-hop overhead, MTU
fragility, not-fixed long-lived-stream failover, and beta status all
push toward the direct in-cluster Service path. **Use the in-cluster
Service for in-cluster callers.**

## 4. NetworkPolicy egress patterns for the OTEL Collector

See [references/networkpolicy-otel-patterns.md](references/networkpolicy-otel-patterns.md)
for full detail.

### CNI context

k3s uses Flannel as default CNI [25]. Flannel does not enforce
NetworkPolicy [26]. k3s embeds kube-router's NPC for enforcement [24]:

> "K3s includes an embedded network policy controller. The underlying
> implementation is kube-router's netpol controller library (no other
> kube-router functionality is present)." [24]

### Pattern A: `ipBlock` on Collector ClusterIP — avoid

Three problems:

1. **ClusterIP is not stable across recreation.** `spec.clusterIP` is
   immutable on a given Service, but Service deletion + recreate (Helm
   reinstall, cluster rebuild) yields a fresh ClusterIP from the pool.
   Tenant Pods silently lose connectivity.
2. **ipBlock behavior with cluster-internal IPs is implementation-
   dependent per spec.** kubernetes.io documents only the node-traffic
   exception [22].
3. **Some CNIs explicitly do not match.** Azure CNI powered by Cilium:

   > "A limitation of Azure CNI Powered by Cilium is that a
   > NetworkPolicy `ipBlock` can't select pod or node IPs." [27]

   k3s+kube-router does match by IP, but the same kube-proxy DNAT
   timing question applies.

### Pattern B: `namespaceSelector` + `podSelector` on otel ns — recommended

```yaml
egress:
- to:
  - namespaceSelector:
      matchLabels:
        kubernetes.io/metadata.name: otel
    podSelector:
      matchLabels:
        app.kubernetes.io/name: opentelemetry-collector
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 4317
```

Three properties make this work:

1. `kubernetes.io/metadata.name` is auto-injected and immutable:

   > "The Kubernetes control plane sets an immutable label
   > `kubernetes.io/metadata.name` on all namespaces. The value of the
   > label is the namespace name." [23]

2. AND-combination in a single `to:` entry narrows to "Collector Pods
   in the otel namespace" rather than the namespace OR Pods OR'd:

   > "A single `to/from` entry that specifies both `namespaceSelector`
   > and `podSelector` selects particular Pods within particular
   > namespaces." [22]

3. CNI-portable. Works identically on Flannel+kube-router, Calico, and
   Cilium (where ipBlock fails) [22][27].

Default OTLP gRPC port is `4317` per the OTEL Collector Helm chart
defaults [28].

### Pattern C: tailnet route — same NetPol shape, against tailscale ns

Mechanically identical to Pattern B; just retargets to the proxy Pod in
the `tailscale` namespace. The decision between B and C is governed by
D3, not by NetPol concerns. Pattern C also exposes a Pod-label that is
Operator-internal and may change across versions — Pattern B against
the Collector's own labels is more stable.

### DNS allowance — independent, mandatory

NetworkPolicy is L3/L4 only [22]. The Pod's call to
`otel-collector.otel.svc.cluster.local:4317` fails at DNS resolution if
default-deny egress excludes kube-system / kube-dns. Required:

```yaml
egress:
- to:
  - namespaceSelector:
      matchLabels:
        kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
    podSelector:
      matchLabels:
        k8s-app: kube-dns
  ports:
  - {protocol: UDP, port: 53}
  - {protocol: TCP, port: 53}
```

UDP AND TCP. The project's NetPol currently excludes the 10/8 range
where CoreDNS lives — without an explicit DNS rule, every in-cluster
DNS lookup fails silently and masquerades as a Collector reachability
problem.

### Verdict

**Pattern B + explicit DNS allowance.** Avoid Pattern A. Pattern C is
mechanically equivalent to B but pointed at the wrong destination per
D3's conclusion.

## 5. Synthesis

See [references/synthesis.md](references/synthesis.md) for the
recommendation per concern with dimension cross-references.

Recap:

- **PVC model:** one StatefulSet per operator with
  `volumeClaimTemplates`; leave `persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy`
  at default Retain/Retain. See [D1](#1-pvc-for-home-statefulset-vs-deploymentpvc).
- **PodSecurity + fsGroup:** stay on `restricted`; use
  `fsGroup` + `fsGroupChangePolicy: OnRootMismatch` for non-root
  ownership; no init container. See
  [D2](#2-pvc-permissions-for-non-root-podsecurity-profile).
- **OTEL route for in-cluster callers:** in-cluster Service
  (`otel-collector.otel.svc.cluster.local:4317`), not the tailnet
  hostname. See
  [D3](#3-tailscale-operator-pod-to-tailnet-egress). Tailnet
  hostname remains correct for external callers.
- **NetworkPolicy pattern:** `namespaceSelector + podSelector` AND'd in
  a single `to:` entry, plus a separate explicit DNS allowance to
  kube-system/kube-dns on UDP+TCP/53. See
  [D4](#4-networkpolicy-egress-patterns-for-the-otel-collector).
- **Cross-cutting:** add `100.64.0.0/10` to the existing egress deny
  ranges once tenant Pods no longer need direct tailnet egress.

The brainstorm session that follows can take these as inputs and design
the actual manifests.

## Limitations and gaps

- The stable GA milestone of `persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy`
  past beta-in-1.27 is implied by the kubernetes.io StatefulSet doc but
  the linked source text was truncated in the fetched page; treat 1.32
  GA as "very likely" pending direct doc verification.
- Whether Longhorn 1.11 uses `DelegateFSGroupToCSIDriver` (and so the
  CSI driver, not kubelet, applies fsGroup) was not verified from
  primary source. The recommendation assumes kubelet-driven fsGroup,
  which is the default.
- The DNSConfig CRD mechanics (the Tailscale Operator's CoreDNS stub-
  domain forwarding pattern) is reported by the discovery agent from
  primary docs but the specific page was not fetched; the "without
  DNSConfig, MagicDNS NXDOMAIN" claim is agent-extracted.
- The exact iptables chain ordering inside k3s's kube-router NPC
  relative to kube-proxy ClusterIP DNAT was not verified. The
  recommendation against Pattern A holds independently (ClusterIP
  recreation issue), but anyone wedded to Pattern A should inspect
  `iptables-save | grep KUBE` ordering.
- The OTEL Collector chart's actual Pod labels were not extracted from
  the chart templates; verify the live labels with `kubectl get pod -n
  otel --show-labels` before pinning Pattern B's podSelector to
  specific values.
- This research did NOT investigate alternatives to PVC-for-HOME
  (ephemeral + git-pull-on-start, restic/S3-backed snapshots) — they
  were explicitly excluded per the prompt. If `$HOME` durability is
  cheap to throw away (e.g., everything is rebuildable from a git
  repo), the entire D1+D2 path can be sidestepped with `emptyDir`.
